t: The top-level products list shows every loaded product ordered by name, each with its number of children.
The folder box and its Browse button are usable only when the 'This folder' choice is selected.

The Semantic Policy fragment shows one section per area the policy applies to: the machine section reads the computer source and its comments, the user section reads the user source and its comments; an area the policy does not cover is left out.
The policy inspector shows a "Registry value" line for the policy only when the policy names a registry value.
The policy inspector shows a "Client extension" line for the policy only when the policy names a client extension.
The support definitions list shows only definitions whose name contains the typed filter text, ignoring upper or lower case; an empty filter shows all.
The policy details window names the section a policy applies to: "User or computer" when it applies to both, "Computer" when machine-only, "User" when user-only.

The support details window states how a support definition matches products: "Match all the referenced products", "Match any of the referenced products", or "Do not match products" when it has no matching logic.

When the ADMX folder dialog opens, 'This folder' is chosen first, and the 'The domain's SYSVOL' choice is available only if the computer is joined to a domain and the folder \\domain\SYSVOL\domain\Policies\PolicyDefinitions exists.
The product details window labels a product "Major revision", "Minor revision" or "Top-level product" from its type.

The detail window of a category shows its parent's name and enables the parent button when the parent exists; when the parent is named but missing it shows "<orphaned from <parent>>" and the button is disabled; a top-level category shows nothing.
Within each section of the fragment, the policy comment is included only when one is stored for that policy, and the option values are included only when the policy is Enabled.
The detail window of a template file lists only the policies, categories (including sub-categories), products (including versions) and support rules that were defined in that file.
Double-clicking the loaded ADMX files list opens the file details for the selected row without checking that a row is selected; pressing Enter does check.
When a policy names a support definition that exists, its name is shown and the support-details button is enabled.

Each entry of a support definition is listed by the name of the nested support definition when it is one, otherwise by the name of the product, otherwise as "<missing: " followed by the product code the entry names.
Double-clicking the support definitions list opens the definition details for the selected row without checking that a row is selected; pressing Enter does check.
The product details window shows a version number for major and minor revisions only; for a top-level product the version is blank.
A product with a parent shows the parent name and enables the parent button; a product with no parent shows a blank parent and the button is disabled.

The major versions list shows the children of the selected top-level product ordered by version, with the heading naming that product; with no product selected it is empty and prompts the person to select one.
When a policy sits in a category that exists, the category name is shown and the category-details button is enabled.
When OK is pressed in the ADMX folder dialog, the folder is the system's Windows PolicyDefinitions folder, the domain SYSVOL folder, or the typed folder, as chosen.
The product details window lists every child revision of a product with its version and name; a product with no children shows an empty list.
The option to clear the workspace before adding the folder is ticked by default, and its choice is passed on only when a folder that exists was accepted.
The fragment text starts with the heading "Policy Plus Semantic Policy" and a blank line only when "Include SPOL header" is ticked; otherwise only the fragment is shown.
Clearing the search forgets the results, so reopening them reports that no search has been run.
Double-clicking a child revision in the product details window shows that child in the same window; with nothing selected, nothing happens.

The minor versions list shows the children of the selected major version ordered by version, with the heading naming it; with no major version selected it is empty and prompts the person to select one.
Double-clicking an entry in the support details window opens the product details window for a product entry, and shows a nested support definition in the same window.
Pressing Escape closes the ADMX folder dialog as cancelled, with no folder chosen.
Opening product details by double-click or Enter does nothing when no product is selected in that list.
In the inspector, a group of affected registry settings with no on or off setting reads "Left implicit" when the policy names a registry value, and "Left to elements" when it names none.
The policy inspector lists presentation details for the policy whenever it has both a presentation and elements, whatever the elements hold.
A category appears in the tree only when it passes the visibility rule; each shown category gets an icon by its kind and carries its visible subcategories below it, and the tree is sorted.
After the category tree is rebuilt from the loaded definitions, no category, policy or highlighted item is selected and the information pane shows the empty state.

When the list is rebuilt, the policy already selected is selected again and revealed only if it is still listed, that is, it sits in the category shown and passes the visibility rule; otherwise nothing is selected.
The right pane lists the chosen category in this order: an "Up: <parent name>" row marked "Parent" when the category has a parent, then visible subcategories by name, then visible policies by name.
The category tree selection follows the category shown in the right pane.

For a list element the inspector states how value names are formed: "User provides value names" when the person names them, a prefix when the element has one, otherwise "No prefix (values named for their data)".
When nothing is selected, the title and support lines are hidden and the pane reads "Select an item to see its description.".
For a selected policy the information pane shows its title, "(no requirements information)" when it has no support rule or "Requirements:" plus the support name, and its explanation.
Choice display names in the inspector are resolved through the definitions file that defines the policy, and choices are numbered from zero in file order.

For a selected or highlighted category the pane shows its title, "This category contains N policies and M subcategories." ("The selected category" when highlighted but not opened) and its explanation.
A category is orphaned when it has no parent among the loaded definitions although its definition names one.
A category is empty when it holds no subcategories and no policies at all, counting hidden ones.
A category's icon is chosen in this order: orphaned, then empty, then normal.
A policy's icon is chosen in this order: preference, then plain when it has no configurable elements, then "extra configuration" when it has some.
The inspector copies the selected line to the clipboard only on Ctrl+C with a line selected.
A category is visible when empty categories are switched on.
A policy is visible only if it applies to a chosen area (user, computer or both).
When a view setting changes, the program moves up to the nearest visible category, drops the selected policy if the move happened or the policy is now hidden, then rebuilds the tree and list.

With both areas shown, a policy that applies to both areas shows its common state followed by "(2)" when both match, the computer state followed by "(C)" when only the user is Not Configured, the user state followed by "(U)" when only the computer is Not Configured, and "Mixed" otherwise.
With both areas shown, a policy that applies to one area shows that area's state followed by "(C)" for computer or "(U)" for user.
A policy's state in one area reads "Enabled", "Disabled", "Not Configured" or "Unknown"; the computer source is read for the computer area and the user source for any other.
With both areas shown, the comment column is empty when neither area has a comment, shows "(multiple)" when both have one, and otherwise shows the single comment.
A policy's comment in one area is empty when that source has no comment file or holds no comment for the policy, and otherwise the saved text.

A policy is a preference, not a managed policy, when it names a registry key outside the three policy locations: software\policies, software\microsoft\windows\currentversion\policies and system\currentcontrolset\policies.

After the edit dialog is accepted, which changes the open policy source in memory only, the list is refreshed in place if the current category is still visible; otherwise the program moves up to the nearest visible category.
Closing the workspace or replacing it with a new one discards all loaded definitions and the previous search results.
A filter on managed policies hides preferences when managed policies are wanted, and hides managed policies when preferences are wanted.
A policy passes the filter only when it passes every active part of it.
A filter on state keeps only policies whose state in the checked area is Configured (Enabled or Disabled), Not Configured, Disabled or Enabled, as chosen.
A filter on comments keeps only policies that have a non-empty comment in the checked area, or only those that have none, as chosen.
A filter on products keeps only policies supported by the chosen products, honouring the options to match any product and to include policies with blank support.
A policy applies to an area when its definition declares that area; a policy declared for both applies to each.

When loading definitions reports no problems nothing is shown; otherwise the person sees "Errors were encountered while adding administrative templates to the workspace." with each problem, and, only where a choice is wanted, is asked "Continue trying to use this workspace?".
The language for definition text is the saved language code, or the computer's own language when none is saved.
Selecting a category in the tree makes it the current category and clears any selected policy.
Highlighting a policy makes it the selected policy and clears any highlighted category; highlighting a category does the reverse; highlighting nothing clears both.
When a definitions folder is opened, the workspace is emptied first only if "clear workspace" is chosen.

A definitions folder is remembered as the definitions folder for the next start only when "clear workspace" was chosen and the load did not fail; when the workspace is added to, the remembered folder is unchanged.
When opening a definitions folder fails, the person is told "The folder could not be fully added to the workspace." with the reason.

A single ADMX file picked from the file dialog (ADMX files only) is added to the current workspace without emptying it and is not remembered as the definitions folder; a failure shows "The ADMX file could not be added to the workspace." with the reason.
Closing the workspace from the menu empties it at once with no confirmation and rebuilds the view.
The "Empty Categories" menu switches empty categories on or off and the view moves to the nearest visible category.
The area choice "User" shows user policies, "Computer" shows computer policies and any other choice shows both.
Opening an item in the policy list does nothing with no selection, opens a category as the current one, or opens a policy's editor for the area currently shown; Enter does the same.
Policy deduplication merges otherwise identical user and computer policy pairs into single policies that apply to both and tells the person "Deduplicated N policies.".
When the right-click menu is opened from the category tree, it is shown for the selected category, and a tree with no selected category is not handled (the program fails with an error).
The right-click menu shows only the actions that fit what was clicked: policy-only actions are hidden for a category, and category-only actions are hidden for a policy.
When a category in the tree is right-clicked, it becomes the selected category, because a right-click alone does not select it; a left-click is left as is.
The text of a policy description is tidied for display: leading and trailing spaces are removed from every line and blank space at the end of the text is dropped.
An XML attribute that is absent gives nothing.
An XML attribute that is absent, or whose text is not valid for the type of the stated default, gives that default.
A policy's lists of on-values and off-values count as enabled or disabled evidence for each value in them that is present, using the list's own key when it names one.
When a language file has no policy resources section, or its revision is missing or not a number, the file is refused as invalid and its template file is not loaded.

A template file is refused as invalid when any of these is missing or unreadable: the policy definitions section; a namespace entry's prefix or namespace; a superseded-ADM file name; a minimum revision (missing or not a number); a support rule's name or display name; a support reference or range without its reference, or a version bound that is not a whole number; a product's name, display name or version index; a category's name or display name; a category's parent entry or its reference when the category has content; a policy's name, display name, key or class; a policy's category or supported-on reference; a number value's value; a list item's value name; a choice item's display name; or an option's id.
Only files directly in the chosen folder whose names end in .admx (in any letter case) are loaded as templates; subfolders and other files are ignored.

A policy with a registry value of its own counts as enabled evidence when that value holds its 'on' value, which is the number 1 when the template gives none, and as disabled evidence when it holds its 'off' value or is marked for deletion when the template gives none.

When a template file is refused with a reported failure (unparsable, invalid, namespace already owned, or no usable language file), it is skipped and the failure is listed; the other files in the folder still load and the structures are built from those that loaded.
The namespace of a template is the one listed as its target; each prefix a template declares must be unique, and a repeated prefix refuses the file as invalid.

A language file's text table is read only from its first text table, and each text is kept under its id; when the same text id appears twice, the file is refused as invalid and its template file is not loaded.

A template's superseded-ADM file name and minimum language revision are read when present; a superseded entry without a file name, or a minimum revision that is missing or not a number, refuses the template as invalid.
Loading a single template file adds that file alone to the policies already loaded, builds the structures, and reports one failure when the file is refused.

When a template file cannot be parsed as XML, it is refused with the message "Couldn't load <path>: The ADMX XML couldn't be parsed: <detail>."; any other read problem is refused with "The ADMX is invalid: <detail>".
A language file's screen layouts are read only from its first presentation table; when the same layout id appears twice, the file is refused as invalid and its template file is not loaded.
For a policy's list elements, a marked-for-deletion list counts as one deleted element, and a list that holds any values counts as a present element and cancels that deletion.

A support rule is 'any of' when its first logic element is "or", 'all of' when it is "and", and blank otherwise; only that first logic element is read, each reference or range in it becomes an entry, and a range may carry a minimum and maximum version.

When a template file's namespace is already held by a template file loaded earlier, it is refused with "The <namespace> namespace is already owned by a different ADMX file", so the same file cannot be added twice.

When a template declares no target namespace, loading the folder stops at once with an error: the files after it are not read, nothing is built, and the person sees the error text (a start-up load also discards the workspace).

The language file for a template is taken from the subfolder named exactly by the language code if it holds this template's file; else from the first subfolder whose name starts with the same language part (before the dash, compared with capital letters mattering) that holds this template's file; else from the en-US subfolder if it holds it.
For a checkbox element: a value marked for deletion counts as one deleted element.
A number box takes default value 1, shows its up-down spinner and steps by 1 unless the language file says otherwise; an unreadable attribute value falls back to the same defaults.
When no language file is found in any of those places, the template file is refused with "The corresponding ADML is missing" and none of its content is loaded.
For any other element (number, text, choice, multi-line text), a value marked for deletion counts as a deleted element and a value that is present counts as a present element.
When the chosen language file cannot be parsed as XML, the template is refused with "The ADML XML couldn't be parsed: <detail>"; any other read problem gives "The ADML is invalid: <detail>".
If any element is present, the elements add their count to the enabled evidence; only when none is present do deleted elements add to the disabled evidence.

When both a template file and its language file load, the template's categories, products, support rules and policies are staged for the next build and the pair is recorded as loaded under the template's namespace.
A check box starts unticked unless the language file marks it ticked.
Products form three levels: a product, its major versions and their minor versions; deeper levels are not read, and each version must carry a version index or the file is refused as invalid.

A policy is Enabled when enabled evidence exceeds disabled evidence, Disabled when disabled exceeds enabled, Not configured when there is no evidence either way, and Unclear when both are equal and above zero.
Entries of a combo box or drop-down list are sorted unless the language file says not to sort them.

A value counts as present when: for a deletion marker, it is marked for deletion; for a number, it exists as a whole number and equals the expected number; for text, it exists as text and equals the expected text.
A drop-down list has a preselected item only when the language file names one; otherwise none is preselected.
A category's explanation is optional.

Only labels, number boxes, text boxes, check boxes, combo boxes, drop-down lists, list boxes and multi-line text boxes are kept in a screen layout; any other control in the language file is dropped without notice.
A list of values counts as present only when every value in it is present.
A control keeps the reference id the language file gives it, which ties it to the matching setting option in the template file; a control without one has no id.
A value in a policy file counts as present only if it is stored and not marked for deletion.

Two policies are merged into one for both sections when they are alone in the same category under the same name, one is for users and the other for computers, and both have the same explanation text and the same registry key; the first is removed and the second becomes a both-sections policy.
Reading a value from a policy file gives nothing when the value is absent or marked for deletion.
A registry value in a template is a delete marker, a number or a text, decided by the first of those it contains; a value with none of them is treated as a delete marker.
A value in a policy file counts as marked for deletion when a deletion marker names it, when the key has a clear-all marker, or when a delete-values list for the key names it, regardless of case.

A policy gets a settings screen layout only when the template names one, the name is written as "$(presentation.<id>)", and the language file holds a layout with that id; in every other case the policy has none.

A category whose parent is named is attached under that parent, found among items of this load or of files loaded earlier; when the parent is not found, the category has no parent but is still listed among the top-level categories.
A semantic policy text line shows 'C' for a machine policy and 'U' for a user policy, followed by the identifier.
When a policy is written as semantic policy text, backslashes in its comment are doubled and each carriage return plus line feed pair is written as '\n'.
A policy's switched-on and switched-off effects are read from its enabled and disabled values and lists; a list entry names a value and optionally its own key, falling back to the list's default key.
A child product (major or minor version) is attached under its parent product, which must be defined in the same template file; only products without a parent are listed as top-level products.
Listing the values of a key in a policy file leaves out the marker entries unless the caller asks for them.
The saved value of a number or text element is read as stored; the reading assumes the value exists and is of the right kind, and is not checked first.
A support rule entry is linked to the product its reference names; when no such product exists it is linked to the support rule of that name; when neither exists it stays unlinked.
When a policy is written as semantic policy text, its settings are listed only if the policy is Enabled.
A list element whose entries have names the person provides is read as every stored name with its value, under the element's key.
In semantic policy text, a whole number is written with a leading #, an unsigned number as digits, and a yes/no value as True or False.
A policy is listed under the category its reference names, found in this load or earlier ones; when that category is not found the policy is kept in the policy list but belongs to no category.

A list element whose entry names do not matter is read as a list of values: when the list has a prefix, the stored values named prefix1, prefix2, and so on, in order, until the first number that is missing; otherwise every stored value name under the key.
A policy shows the 'supported on' rule its reference names, found in this load or earlier ones; when none is found it has none.

When the structures are built, all new categories, products, support rules and policies join the final lists and the staged items are cleared, so loading further files adds to what is already available.
A choice element is read as the position of the first item whose own value is present and, when the item has a value list, whose list is wholly present; when no item matches, the position is -1.
A policy applies to computers when its class is "Machine", to users when "User", and to both for any other class value.
The saved value of a multi-line text element is read as stored, without first checking that it exists.
A policy takes its category and its 'supported on' rule from the references in its own content, and has options only when it contains an options section.
A checkbox is on when its on value (or all values of its on list) is present, or, with neither defined, when its value is 1; it is off in every other case, including when its off value is present.
A name or description written as "$(string.<id>)" shows the language file's text for that id; an unknown id shows the code itself; any other text is shown as written; an empty value stays empty.

A number option accepts 0 to 4,294,967,295 unless the template sets other limits, overwrites existing values unless marked soft, and is stored as a number unless marked as text; unreadable attribute values fall back to these defaults.
A yes/no option takes its registry effect for true and false from true and false values and lists.
An item's unique name is its template's namespace, a colon and its own name, so equal names in different templates stay apart.
A text option allows 255 characters, is optional, is stored as plain text and overwrites existing values unless the template says otherwise; unreadable attribute values fall back to these defaults.

A reference containing a colon uses the namespace the template declared for its prefix; with an unknown prefix it is taken as already complete; a reference without a colon belongs to the template's own namespace.
A REG file cannot be used as a source for asking whether a value is present: the request fails with 'not implemented'.

A list option replaces other entries of its key unless marked additive, stores plain text unless marked expandable, numbers entries automatically unless the template says the person names them, and counts as prefixed only when a value prefix is given.
A REG file cannot be used as a source for reading a value: the request fails with 'not implemented'.
A REG file cannot be used as a source for checking whether a value will be deleted: the request fails with 'not implemented'.
A REG file cannot be used as a source for listing a key's values: the request fails with 'not implemented'.
A choice option is optional unless marked required.
Text read from a policy file stops at its first empty character, and a multiple-string value ends at its first empty string.
A policy option of any kind other than number, yes/no, text, list, choice or multi-line text is dropped without notice.
An option's registry value name is taken from its own value name, except for a list option that has a value prefix attribute: the prefix is used and the own value name only when that prefix is empty.
A stored policy file value is read back as text for text and expandable text, a 32-bit or 64-bit number for numbers, a list of strings for multiple strings, and raw bytes for every other type.
When a policy lists no supported-on information, it counts as supported only if the caller allows unlisted policies.
A value in the live registry counts as present when its key exists and, unless the value name is empty, the key lists a value of that name, regardless of case.
A support entry for a product counts as met in two cases.

A support entry for a product that has versions beneath it, whether a version range or a plain entry for a parent product that is not itself chosen, counts as met when any version in its range, or a sub-product directly beneath one, is chosen.
Reading a value from the live registry gives nothing when the key is missing.
A support definition met a second time anywhere in one evaluation counts as not met, because the list of definitions seen is never emptied.
When the caller asks for 'any' matching, a support definition whose logic is all-of needs every entry met, and any other definition needs one entry met.
The live registry never reports a value as marked for deletion.

A registry key counts as a policy key when it is one of the three policy branches (software\policies, software\microsoft\windows\currentversion\policies, system\currentcontrolset\policies) or lies below one, regardless of case.
When the build script runs, it replaces the program's version in a generated source file with the text git gives for the current commit.

Open File puts the whole chosen file into the text box, replacing what was typed without asking and without checking it; Reset, after a Yes to "Are you sure you want to reset the text box?", restores the header "Policy Plus Semantic Policy" and blank lines.
Verify reads the SPOL text and reports "Validation successful, N policy settings found." or "SPOL validation failed: " followed by the reason; nothing is applied.
Closing the policy setting dialog with Cancel is reported as a change when Apply was used earlier in that session, and as a cancel otherwise.
Apply accepts only SPOL text that reads correctly; the parsed file is passed back to the main window.
The Supported on box shows the supported-on name of the policy and is empty when the policy names none.

A policy that applies to both computer and user can be edited for either, starting on Computer when no section was given; a policy for one section is fixed to that section and the section choice is unavailable.
Opening Import SPOL discards any previously parsed SPOL so a cancelled session passes nothing back.
When the list editor is confirmed for a list where the person names each entry, and two entries have exactly the same name, it is refused with "Multiple entries are named "<name>"!
Pressing Escape closes Import SPOL as cancelled unless text in the box is selected; when it is, Escape closes nothing.

When the list editor is confirmed for a list without names, every row except the empty new row at the bottom is returned in the order shown, with no check that a cell has content; a row whose value cell was never filled is returned as an empty entry.
A number entered with a spin box is limited to the minimum and maximum the policy defines, in steps the presentation sets, and starts at the presentation's default.
A plain number box keeps any text a whole-number reading accepts, including a leading sign or spaces; other text is replaced by the default.
Keys other than digits and control keys are ignored in a numeric text box.
A plain text entry is limited to the maximum length the policy defines and starts with the presentation's default text.
A check box starts with the presentation's default state.

A text entry with suggestions is limited to the maximum length the policy defines, starts with the presentation's default text, and lists the presentation's suggestions, sorted unless the presentation turns sorting off.

A drop-down list shows the policy's choices by their translated names, sorted unless the presentation turns sorting off, and preselects the default choice when the presentation names one; otherwise nothing is selected.
The state shown when the dialog opens follows the policy's present state in the source being edited: Enabled, Disabled, or Not Configured for anything else, including an unclear state.

When the policy is Enabled, each option control is set to the value found in the source: numbers into number boxes, text into text and combo boxes, the matching item in drop-downs, true or false into check boxes, lines into multi-line boxes and the stored list into the list editor.
OK and Apply are available only when the chosen policy source can be written to.
The comment box is disabled and reads "Comments unavailable for this policy source" when the source has no comments; otherwise it shows the policy's stored comment, or is empty when there is none.

Applying a policy first forgets everything the source holds for it; Enabled then writes every option's current value, Disabled writes the disabled state, and Not Configured leaves the policy with no values.
When Enabled is chosen, applying writes every option of the policy whatever its value, including options never filled in.
When a policy is applied and the source supports comments, an empty comment box removes the policy's stored comment and any text replaces or adds it.
Option controls can be edited only while Enabled is chosen; with Disabled or Not Configured they are greyed out.
Choosing Computer or User in the dialog switches the source, its writability and its comments to that section, and reloads the chosen state (Enabled, Disabled or Not Configured) from it.
OK writes the policy to the source and closes the dialog as a change.
Apply writes the policy to the source, keeps the dialog open and records that a change was made.
When the policy setting dialog is closed by any other means, it is still reported as a change if Apply was used earlier.

Importing semantic policy applies all its policies to both sources and comments; the person sees "Semantic Policy successfully applied." or "N out of M could not be applied." when some failed, and the view refreshes either way.
When a semantic policy script fails to load, the error gives the line it stopped at, in the form '(Error found on line N.)'.
A semantic policy script is read in lines separated by carriage return and line feed.
A semantic policy script is refused unless its first line is 'Policy Plus Semantic Policy', with the message 'Incorrect signature.'.
A policy header line in a semantic policy script is a user policy only when its first word is exactly 'U'.
A comment line in a semantic policy script is recognised without regard to letter case.
A comment in a semantic policy script is refused when it ends with a lone backslash, with the message 'Escape sequence started at end of comment.'.
The state in a semantic policy script must be 'Not configured', 'Enabled' or 'Disabled', regardless of case. Anything else is refused with 'Unknown policy state.'.
Settings are read only for a policy that is Enabled.
When a value is marked for deletion in a policy file, any value or marker already held under that name is dropped first.
A setting value in a semantic policy script is read in this order.
When a value is forgotten in a policy file, both the value and its deletion marker are removed, so the policy reverts to not saying anything about it.
When a value is set in a policy file, it replaces any value already held under that name.
A bracketed setting in a semantic policy script holds one line per entry.

A source is writable by default for Scratch space; for a registry source it is 'no writing' when the write test failed; for others it is 'no commit' when the file or hive could not be opened for writing.
When a policy file is clearing a key, all values and markers under the key are dropped and a single clear-all marker is stored.
When a semantic policy script is applied to many policies, a policy that fails is skipped and counted, and the rest are still applied.
When a key's clearance is forgotten in a policy file, every clear-all marker for that key is removed.
A semantic policy script applies each policy to the machine source or the user source by its section.
When a semantic policy is applied, a comment is stored for the policy first, only if one is given and a comment store exists, before the old settings are wiped and the new ones written.
When a semantic policy is applied, the policy's earlier settings are wiped first and then the stated state and settings are written.

The registry values a policy touches are its own value, those in its value lists, those of its elements (the whole key for list elements) and those of checkbox and choice sub-lists, each counted once.
When a value is saved into a REG file, it is ignored if a source branch is set and its key lies outside that branch.
A REG file cannot be used as a source for forgetting a value: the request fails with 'not implemented'.
Text stored in a policy file is written in two-byte characters followed by a closing empty character.
When a value is deleted in a REG file, the request is ignored if a source branch is set and the key lies outside it, or if the key is already marked for removal.
When a key is cleared in a REG file, the request is ignored if a source branch is set and the key lies outside it.
When a policy is forgotten, the whole key of each of its list elements is cleared and every registry value it touches is dropped from the source, so it reads as Not configured.
When a key's clearance is forgotten in a REG file, the key-removal entry is dropped if it exists.
A 32-bit number is stored in a policy file as 4 bytes, lowest byte first.
When a registry value is written for a policy, a value defined as 'delete' is removed, a numeric value is saved as a 32-bit number and a text value as a text string.
A 64-bit number is stored in a policy file as 8 bytes, lowest byte first.
When a policy is set to Not configured or Unknown, SetPolicyState writes and removes nothing.
A multiple-string value is stored as its strings each followed by an empty character, with one more empty character closing the list.
When a policy is set to Enabled and the policy has a registry value name but defines no explicit on value, the value is saved as the number 1.
When a policy is set to Enabled, its own on value is saved and any extra values listed for the on state are saved with it.
When a policy is set to Enabled, only the settings the person supplied are written.
A setting that names its own registry key is saved under that key. Otherwise it is saved under the policy's key.
When a number setting is saved, it is written as text if the definition says to store it as text, otherwise as a 32-bit number.
When a checkbox setting is saved, a ticked box with no defined on value first saves the number 1, and an unticked box with no defined off value first removes the value.
When a text setting is saved, it is written as an expandable text string if the definition says so, otherwise as a plain text string.
When a list setting is saved and the definition does not say to keep other entries, every existing value under the list's key is removed first.
When a list setting is saved, entries that carry their own names are saved under those names.
A value written to a policy file is stored as text, expandable text, a 32-bit or 64-bit number or a multiple string by its stated type.
When a choice setting is saved, the value of the chosen item is saved together with any extra values that item lists.
When a multi-line text setting is saved, it is written as a multiple-string value.
When a policy is set to Disabled and the definition gives no off value, its registry value is removed.
When a policy is set to Disabled, each setting gets only its own removal.
When a value is deleted in the live registry and its key does not exist, nothing happens. A missing value is not an error.
In the live registry, 'forgetting' a value deletes it, because the registry cannot remember a pending deletion.
When a number is saved to the live registry, an unsigned 32-bit or 64-bit number is converted to the signed number the registry stores with the same bits, and the key is created if missing.
Clearing a key in the live registry deletes every value in it but leaves the key and its subkeys. Forgetting a key's clearance does nothing.
A name typed in the user dialog is turned into the account's security identifier (SID) on Search; if the name cannot be translated, the person is told "The name could not be translated to a SID."
When OK is pressed with a name typed but no SID, the name is looked up first, and the dialog stays open if no SID results.
When OK is pressed, the SID text must be a valid SID or the person is told "The SID is not valid.
In the user hive dialog, OK does nothing until a folder is selected; then it returns the path C:\Users\<folder>\ntuser.dat and closes.
Pressing Escape closes the user dialog as cancelled.
Pressing Escape closes the user hive dialog as cancelled.
The file picker for a POL file accepts only '.pol' files, allows choosing a file that does not exist yet, and does not ask before an existing file is chosen.
The registry path, POL file name and Browse button for the computer side are usable only when their own choice is selected.
The registry path, POL file name, SID and hive path boxes (and their Browse buttons) for the user side are usable only when their own choice is selected.
When OK is pressed, the computer source is created from the selected choice: Local GPO, Registry (path typed), POL file (name typed), or Scratch space when none of the others is selected.
When OK is pressed, the user source is created from the selected choice: Local GPO, Registry, POL file, per-user GPO (SID typed), user hive (file path typed), or Scratch space otherwise.
Pressing Escape closes the policy sources dialog as cancelled.
Opening new policy sources first closes the ones already open.
A policy source's writability is described as "is fully writable", "cannot be saved" (changes work in memory only) or "cannot be modified"; anything but fully writable counts as a problem.
A source's comments are used only when it has a comment file location.

After opening, if either source is not fully writable the person is told "Not all policy sources are fully writable." with the state of the user and the computer source; if both are fully writable, "Both the user and computer policy sources are loaded and writable." appears only when opening was not quiet (never at start).
Closing the policy sources tells the person "Cleanup did not complete fully because the loaded resources are open in other programs." when any source could not release its resources.
After the person chooses policy sources, they are opened with the opening result shown, and the view moves to the nearest visible category.
A source's comment list is saved to its comment file location whenever the list exists, even when empty; a source without comment support has no list and is skipped.

Saving writes each source's comments first, then writes a source only if it is fully writable (otherwise reported as "not writable"), then remembers the chosen source types and locations for the next start.
The computer counts as having the Group Policy infrastructure only when the number Windows gives for its edition equals one of 59 fixed codes in a list.

A comment file is refused as unreadable when it has no comment-definitions section, a namespace entry without a prefix, a comment without a policy reference, a text without an id, or a repeated prefix, policy reference or text id.

The path of a policy source is fixed by its kind: Local GPO uses the Registry.pol file of the system's local Group Policy (user or machine folder) and its gpt.ini; a per-user GPO uses the folder named by the person's SID under GroupPolicyUsers; a POL file and a user hive use the path given; Scratch space has none.

A registry source must start with HKCU, HKEY_CURRENT_USER, HKU, HKEY_USERS, HKLM or HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE (any case); otherwise it is refused with "The root key is not valid." A path after the root is opened, and created if missing.
A policy file is refused when it does not start with the 'PReg' signature, with the message 'Missing PReg signature'.
A policy file is refused when its format version is not 1, with the message 'Unknown (newer) version of POL format'.

When comments are saved, each comment gets its own text id built from the policy's namespace, policy name and a running number, and each distinct namespace gets a prefix made from its name (dots turned into underscores) and the running number.
When a policy file is read, an extra empty character after the value name, as Microsoft's documentation allows, is skipped.
A registry source counts as writable only when a test value can be written under Software\Policies and removed again; otherwise it is read-only.
When a policy file is read and the same key and value name occur twice, the later entry wins.
A user hive source is mounted by loading the hive file under a fresh temporary name in the machine registry, after the backup and restore privileges are switched on.

No comment of a comment file can be read when any comment's policy reference has no colon or a prefix that is not declared, its text is not written as "$(resource.<id>)", its text id is missing, or two comments resolve to the same policy.
When a policy file is saved, entries are written in alphabetical order, so a key-clearing marker is always written before the values it clears.
A Scratch space source is an empty policy store that can be changed but is never saved anywhere.
Saving comments writes every comment and text held in memory into the target file, in schema version 1.0, replacing what the file held before.
A source read through the file branch covers a POL file, the local Group Policy and a per-user Group Policy, each with a Registry.pol path.

When the Registry.pol of a POL file source, the local Group Policy or a per-user Group Policy does not exist, it is created empty with its folder and treated as writable; a mistyped SID therefore creates a new folder and empty file under the per-user policy folder.
When a source is closed, a mounted user hive is unloaded and the result tells whether unloading succeeded; every other kind of source closes successfully.

Saving a local Group Policy source writes the Registry.pol file, raises the gpt.ini version, and then, on Windows editions that list as having Group Policy (decided by a fixed list of product edition codes), asks Windows to refresh policy ("saved to disk and invoked policy refresh").

Saving a POL file source writes the file only ("saved to disk"); a registry source reports "already applied" because it was changed live; a user hive reports "will apply when policy source is closed"; Scratch space reports "discarded".
Saving a per-user GPO writes its Registry.pol file, raises its gpt.ini version and asks Windows to refresh user policy ("saved to disk and invoked policy refresh").

The comment file for a source sits beside its file: the POL file or hive path with the extension changed to .cmtx; for Local GPO or per-user GPO a file named comment.cmtx in the same folder; for the registry a file under the person's local application data folder (one for user, one for machine); Scratch space has none, so comments are unavailable.
When a policy file's changes are applied to another source, an entry named '**del.' plus a value name deletes that value, using the lower-case key and value names.
When a policy file's changes are applied to another source, an entry starting '**delvals' clears the whole key, using the lower-case key name.
When a policy file's changes are applied to another source, an entry named '**deletevalues' deletes each value in its semicolon-separated list, using lower-case names.
When a policy file's changes are applied to another source, an entry starting '**deletekeys' clears each key named in its semicolon-separated list under the entry's key, using lower-case names.
When a policy file's changes are applied to another source, an entry is saved only if it has a non-empty value name that does not start with '**'.

When a newer policy file is applied over an older one, values the old file held and the new one dropped are forgotten in the target, but only if they sit under the three policy branches of the registry.
When gpt.ini is updated and already exists, its Version number is raised by 1 for a machine source and by 65536 for a user source; if no Version line exists, it is set to 65537 (both parts at 1).
When gpt.ini is updated, the Machine and User extension-name lines for the registry policy are added if missing and left untouched if present.
When gpt.ini does not exist, a new one is written with the General section, both extension-name lines and Version 65537.
The source name shown in the status bar is Local GPO, Registry, File, User GPO, User hive or Scratch space, followed by the path or SID in brackets when there is one.
In the section dialog, OK does nothing until User or Computer is chosen; then it returns that section and closes.
A number entered for a registry value is limited to 0 to 4,294,967,295 for a 32-bit value and to 0 to 18,446,744,073,709,551,615 for a 64-bit value.
The registry prefix box in the export dialog starts as HKEY_CURRENT_USER\ when the user policy source is being edited and HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\ otherwise.
The new registry value dialog offers the types String, Expandable string, List of strings, 32-bit DWord and 64-bit QWord, and starts on String.

When a REG file is chosen and the prefix is empty, the prefix is guessed from the file; if the file holds default values, the person is warned "This REG file contains data for default values, which cannot be applied to all policy sources."
Only files of type *.reg are offered by the file chooser when browsing for the REG file.
Pressing Escape closes the section dialog as cancelled.

The raw policy file editor lists keys in alphabetical order ignoring case, each followed by its sub-keys indented, then its values in alphabetical order; a value with an empty name (the marker that keeps an empty key) is not listed.

When Delete is confirmed with the option to clear the key or to delete all values under it, the choice is accepted without further input; no option is chosen when the dialog opens, and confirming with none chosen does nothing.
When the key name dialog is confirmed, the typed name is returned unchecked; when it is cancelled, an empty name is returned, so an empty typed name and a cancel look the same to the caller.
When Delete is confirmed with the option to delete one value and the value name is empty, it is refused and the person is told "You must enter a value name."; with a name, the choice is accepted.
The section dialog lets a person choose only the sections the caller allows: User and Computer are each usable only when enabled by the caller.
When the guess fails, the person is only warned "An error occurred while trying to guess the prefix." and the prefix stays empty.
Export to a registry script is refused until a file name is given; the person is told "Please specify a filename and path for the exported REG."
The value name box in the delete dialog can be typed in only while the option to delete one value is chosen.
Pressing Escape closes Import REG as cancelled.
When the registry script is written, the person is told "REG exported successfully." and the dialog closes; on any failure they are told only "Failed to export REG!" and the dialog stays open.

Special deletion entries in a policy file are listed as such: "**deletevalues" as "Delete values" with its data, "**del.<name>" as "Delete value" with the name, and entries starting "**delvals" as "Delete all values".
Import is refused with "Please specify a REG file to import." when no file is named, and with "Please specify the prefix used to fully qualify paths in the REG file." when no prefix is given.
Import loads the REG file with the prefix and applies it straight to the chosen policy source; on any failure the person is told only "Failed to import the REG file."
When a typed hexadecimal number is too large to fit, the value is set to the largest allowed value; text that is not a hexadecimal number leaves the value unchanged.
Ordinary values are listed with their content: lists of text joined by spaces, text as it is, 32-bit and 64-bit numbers in decimal, binary data as hexadecimal bytes separated by spaces.
Pressing Done (or Enter) closes the raw policy editor as accepted, and pressing Escape closes it as cancelled; there is no Cancel button.
A new key name is refused with "The key name is not valid." when it contains a backslash.
A new key name is refused with "The key name is already taken." when a key of that name, ignoring case, already exists under the same parent.

Adding a key does nothing when the name is left empty or the dialog is cancelled; otherwise the key is created under the selected key, or at the top level when nothing is selected, as an empty key, and is selected in the list.
Editing a value offers a text, number or list-of-text dialog by kind: text kinds (plain and expandable) a text box, 32-bit and 64-bit numbers a number box, lists of text a multi-line box.

Adding a value to the selected key lets the person choose a name and one of five kinds; the starting data is empty text, zero, or an empty list by kind, and the value is stored only if the person then confirms its data.
Deleting a key offers three choices, and OK does nothing until one is chosen; cancelling or Escape changes nothing.

Deleting a single value from the list does not erase it from the file: it is replaced by a deletion entry named "**del." followed by the value name, which removes the value on the machine when policies are applied.

Forgetting a key asks "Are you sure you want to remove this key and all its contents?" and, on Yes, removes the key, all its sub-keys, every value and every clearing mark from the file with no deletion left behind; No changes nothing.
Editing a value replaces its data with the confirmed new data and keeps its name and kind; the value stays selected.
When nothing is selected in the policy file's list, only Add key and Export are available; Add value, Delete value, Edit and Forget are unavailable.
When a key is selected in the list, Add key, Add value, Delete value, Forget and Export are available, and Edit is unavailable.

When a value is selected in the list, only Forget is always available; Add key, Add value and Export are unavailable, and Edit and Delete value are available only when the value is not already a delete marker.
The export dialog starts with the selected key as its source branch, or empty when nothing is selected.
Exporting uses a source backed by a POL file as is.
When a POL is built from a registry-backed source, every value and every sub-key under each of the three policy locations is copied with its own data type, with environment variables left unexpanded.
Importing a POL file applies it to the source the person chooses (user or computer).
Exporting a POL file writes the chosen area's policy source as a POL file; the person sees "POL exported successfully." or "The POL file could not be saved.".

Raw POL editing is available only when the user or computer source is backed by a POL file, otherwise the person is told "Neither loaded source is backed by a POL file."; the area chosen is limited to POL-backed sources.
The first time raw POL editing is used, the person must accept "Caution!
Exporting to a registry file (REG) hands the policy source of the area the person chooses, as a POL, to the export dialog.
Importing a registry file (REG) applies it to the policy source of the area the person chooses and refreshes the view.
Blank lines and lines starting with a semicolon in a REG file are ignored.
A REG file is refused when its first line is not 'Windows Registry Editor Version 5.00', with the message 'Incorrect REG signature'.
A REG key header starting with a minus sign marks the whole key for removal. Otherwise it opens a key whose values follow.
A REG file value line starting with an at sign is the key's default value, with an empty name.
In a REG file, a value written as a bare minus sign is a value to delete.
When a REG file is written, a default value is shown as an at sign, and quotes and backslashes in names and text are escaped.
Keys marked for removal are written to a REG file with a leading minus sign and values marked for deletion as a bare minus sign.
Applying a whole policy file to a source applies it as the difference from an empty file, so nothing is forgotten.
A REG key name is shortened by the prefix only when it starts with it, regardless of case. A prefix always ends in a backslash.
A key name in a policy file is listed as a subkey only once, regardless of case, and the requested key itself is never listed.
When a REG file is applied to a source, a key marked for removal is cleared, a value marked for deletion is deleted and any other value is saved.
A branch name given as the source of a REG export has any trailing backslash removed.
The prefix of a REG file is guessed from its first key only.
A REG file is reported as holding default values when any value has an empty name.
When Search is pressed with both the key and the value empty, the search is refused and the person is told "Please enter search terms."
Starting a search clears earlier results, sets the progress range to the number of policies, and begins on "Starting search".
When Search is pressed with the search text empty, the search is refused and the person is told "Please enter search terms."
When the key text starts with HKLM\, HKCU\, HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\ or HKEY_CURRENT_USER\, the search is refused with "Policies' root keys are determined only by their section.
When none of In title, In description and In comment is ticked, the search is refused with "At least one attribute must be searched.
A policy matches a registry search when at least one registry value it reads or writes meets every term entered; matching ignores case.
A value-name term must match the whole value name; "*" and "?" act as wildcards, so without them the name must be equal.
Text typed in Find by ID is trimmed and looked up in this order: category, product, support definition, then policy.

When the filter dialog opens, the Policy type choice shows Any if the current filter has no policy-type condition, Policy if it keeps only managed policies, and Preference if it keeps only the others.
When the text matches nothing, nothing is selected and a "not found" icon is shown; when the text is empty a blank icon is shown instead.
A key term containing "*" or "?" must match the whole key path as a wildcard pattern.
Search text is split at spaces into plain words, wildcard words (containing "*" or "?") and quoted phrases.
A key term containing a backslash but no wildcard matches policies whose key path starts with that text.

When search results are opened from the main window and no search has been run (or it was cleared), the person is told "No search has been run yet, so there are no results to display." and nothing opens.
When the filter dialog opens, the Current state choice shows Any if the current filter has no state condition, otherwise Not Configured, Configured, Enabled or Disabled as the filter holds.
A key term with no backslash and no wildcard matches policies having a key path with a part equal to that text.
A phrase opened with a double quote runs until a later word ending in a double quote; a phrase never closed is dropped without telling the person, which widens the search.
A policy ID may end with "@U" to mean the user section or "@C" to mean the computer section; without a suffix, or with any other suffix, the policy applies to both sections.
When the filter dialog opens, the Commented choice shows Any if the current filter has no comment condition, Yes if it keeps only commented policies and No if it keeps only uncommented ones.
Taking the next policy returns nothing when no search has run or when the last result has been passed; otherwise it returns the result after the last chosen one.

When the current filter has no supported-on condition, the dialog opens with Supported on unticked, both "Match a policy if at least one selected product is supported" and "Match policies with missing or blank support definitions" ticked, and no product ticked.
A text is a hit only when it contains every plain word as a whole word, every wildcard matching some word, and every quoted phrase as whole words together.

When the current filter has a supported-on condition, the dialog opens with Supported on ticked, exactly the filter's products ticked and the two matching options set as the filter holds; product branches whose tick differs from their parent are opened.
Go closes Find by ID as accepted whether or not the text matched anything, so the caller may receive no selection.
A policy matches when the ticked attributes hit: its title, its description, or a comment on it from any supplied comment source (user or computer).
Pressing Escape closes Find by ID as cancelled.
The search tests every policy in turn, and adds every hit to the list with its category name, in the order policies are held.
The list and progress are refreshed after every 20 policies: "Searching: checked N policies so far, found M hits".
The product requirement box (the product tree and the two matching options) can be used only while Supported on is ticked; it starts unusable.
Pressing Escape closes the filter dialog as cancelled and the current filter is unchanged.
Reset returns every choice to its default: Any for type, state and comment, Supported on unticked, both matching options ticked and no product ticked.
When a search ends it reports "Finished searching: checked N policies, found M hits", or "Search canceled: ..." if stopped, and the Stop button is disabled.
When OK is pressed, the new filter keeps only managed policies for Policy, only unmanaged ones for Preference, and no policy-type condition for Any.
Stop, or closing the results window, cancels the search; closing also leaves the label at "Search canceled" with the bar full if the search had not finished.
When OK is pressed, the new filter requires the chosen state: Not Configured, Configured, Enabled or Disabled; Any sets no state condition.
When the results window is reopened, the previously selected result is selected again if it is still in the list.
When OK is pressed, the new filter keeps only commented policies for Yes, only uncommented ones for No, and no comment condition for Any.
When OK is pressed with Supported on ticked, the filter records every ticked product and both matching options; with it unticked, any ticks and options are discarded and no support condition applies.
Go, or a double-click on a result, accepts only when a result is selected; the selected policy is passed back and its position remembered.
Ticking or unticking a product by hand ticks or unticks every product beneath it to match; changes made by the dialog itself do not spread.
Double-clicking a product checkbox does nothing, so a tick shown always agrees with the tick kept.
The Deduplicate Policies menu entry is hidden, so the person cannot start it.
A search dialog opens either empty or running a new search.
Moving to a policy first shows its category, but only when that category is visible in the tree; otherwise nothing happens and the person is not told.
The area choice offers only "User or Computer", "User" and "Computer", with no free text.
Only one item in the policy list can be selected at a time.
After finding by identifier, a category opens if it is visible, otherwise the person is told "The category is not currently visible.
A policy found by identifier opens in the lower-numbered of the area shown and the area found (computer is lower than user, user lower than both), so Computer wins over User.
Find by text starts a search with what the person entered, and can search both areas' comments.
"Search Results" only reopens the last results and starts no new search.
Find Next moves to the next result that is currently visible, skipping hidden ones, and tells the person "There are no more results that match the filter." when none is left.
Find by registry starts a search with what the person entered.
Changing the filter options turns on "Only Filtered Policies" and moves to the nearest visible category.
The "Only Filtered Policies" menu switches the filter on or off and moves to the nearest visible category.
Choosing a folder in the browse dialog replaces the destination; cancelling the dialog leaves the destination unchanged.
When the person closes the download window while a download is running, the close is refused; the window closes only when no download is running.

Each time the download window opens, the destination folder is set to the Windows policy definitions folder (the PolicyDefinitions folder under the Windows folder) and no new policy folder is reported to the caller.

While a download runs, the start button, close button, destination box and browse button are all disabled, so a second download cannot be started and the destination cannot change; they are enabled again when it ends.

The welcome offer to download policy definitions is considered only once: the first time the window is shown the program records that it has been considered, even when no offer is made, and never considers it again.
When the offer is considered, it is made only if this Windows edition has no Group Policy support and more than two non-empty categories name a parent that is not among the loaded definitions.
When files are moved into a folder, the folder is created if missing and every file already there with the same name is deleted first and then replaced by the new one, with no backup.

For an administrator, each folder handed to the file move that already exists, the destination itself and any existing language folder, has its ownership taken; a language folder created during the move instead inherits permissions from the folder above.

Starting the download always fetches one fixed Microsoft package, the Windows 11 September 2026 Update (26H2) administrative templates, into a scratch folder under the person's local application data as "W11Admx.msi"; the person cannot choose another version.
The downloaded package is unpacked with the Windows installer tool; if the tool ends with a non-zero code the download stops with "Failed to extract the package." and the package is kept.
Before any file is moved, when the folder written in the destination box already exists and the person is an administrator, ownership of it is taken and Administrators are given full control.

The template files are moved into the destination, then the language files for the person's regional format language (the culture of the regional settings, which can differ from the display language) are moved into a folder of that name if the package holds one.
After a successful download the scratch folder is deleted, the person is asked "ADMX files downloaded successfully.

When any step fails, the person is told "Failed to " followed by the step that failed (create a scratch space, download the package, extract the package, take control of the destination, move the ADMX files, remove temporary files); the window stays open, controls are re-enabled, and no policy folder is reported.
After a successful download of definitions, the workspace is emptied, the downloaded folder loaded and saved as the definitions folder, and the view rebuilt; with no new folder nothing changes.

When the policy sources dialog opens with the last-used sources, each side is set to the remembered kind (Local GPO, Registry, POL file, Scratch space, and for users also per-user GPO or user hive), and the registry path, file name, SID or hive path is filled in only for the kinds that carry one.

When the person confirms the language dialog with text that does not split into exactly two parts around a hyphen (for example "en" or "en-US-x"), it is refused with "Please enter a valid language code." and stays open.

When the entered language code, spaces trimmed, is exactly equal (upper and lower case count as different, so en-us differs from en-US) to the stored code, taken without trimming, the dialog closes as cancelled.
The program allows secure connections using TLS 1.0, 1.1 and 1.2 only, so downloads use no other protocol.
On first start, when no policy sources were saved, both the user source and the computer source open as the local Group Policy files (Local GPO) with no extra location.
When the previously saved policy sources cannot be opened, the person is told "The previous policy sources are not accessible.
The list of areas starts on "User or Computer", the first choice, so both user and computer policies are shown at start.
The definitions folder to load is the one saved last time; when none is saved it is the Windows PolicyDefinitions folder.
When loading the saved definitions reports problems, the person is asked whether to keep using the workspace.
When the saved folder is not the Windows default and fails to load, the person is told "Policy definitions could not be loaded from "<folder>": <reason> Load from the default location?".
When the Windows default folder itself fails to load, or fails to load after the person chose Yes, the person is told "Policy definitions could not be loaded: <reason>" and the workspace stays empty.
When the person chooses to load the default location, the workspace is replaced by an empty one and the Windows default folder is loaded into it.
The About box names the author and the GitHub address, and adds the version only when a version was built into the program.
Setting the language saves the new language code at once, then asks "Language changes will take effect when ADML files are next loaded.

When the program's settings area in the registry cannot be opened or created, the program carries on without it: settings read as their defaults, changes are dropped, and the person is not told, so settings are not remembered between runs.
